headings.title: Introduction and Indications for Mechanical Ventilation
headings.content: Mechanical ventilation is a life-saving supportive therapy utilized in clinical settings to assist or completely replace spontaneous breathing when a patient's respiratory system fails to maintain adequate gas exchange. In Nigerian clinical practice, as in global healthcare, understanding the fundamental indications for initiating mechanical ventilation is crucial for nursing students and critical care nurses. Broadly, the indications fall into two main categories: acute respiratory failure (which is further subdivided into hypoxemic and hypercapnic failure) and the need to protect the airway or reduce the work of breathing. Hypoxemic respiratory failure, often seen in conditions like severe pneumonia, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), or pulmonary edema, occurs when the lungs fail to oxygenate arterial blood effectively despite supplemental oxygen. Conversely, hypercapnic respiratory failure involves inadequate alveolar ventilation, leading to a dangerous buildup of carbon dioxide, commonly observed in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) exacerbations, severe asthma, neuromuscular disorders, or drug overdoses. Additionally, patients with depressed mental status due to head trauma, stroke, or general anesthesia are unable to protect their upper airway against aspiration, necessitating invasive mechanical support. Furthermore, severe exhaustion of the respiratory muscles due to prolonged labored breathing can precipitate cardiopulmonary arrest if mechanical intervention is delayed. Recognizing these clinical indicators promptly allows nurses to anticipate equipment needs, prepare emergency resuscitation trolleys, and participate effectively in rapid endotracheal intubation and ventilator setup.

headings.title: Basic Physiology and Mechanics of Breathing
headings.content: To effectively care for a patient on a mechanical ventilator, nursing students must understand the underlying physiology and mechanics of normal breathing versus positive pressure ventilation. Normal spontaneous breathing operates via negative pressure ventilation. During inspiration, the contraction of the diaphragm and intercostal muscles increases the thoracic cavity volume. This action lowers the intrapleural pressure below atmospheric pressure, creating a pressure gradient that draws air passively into the lungs. Exhalation is normally a passive process driven by the elastic recoil of the lung tissue and chest wall. In contrast, mechanical ventilators deliver air into the patient's lungs using positive pressure. Instead of pulling air in by creating negative pressure, the machine forces gas into the airways during inspiration, increasing alveolar pressure above atmospheric pressure. This positive pressure shift fundamentally alters cardiovascular physiology. Because intrathoracic pressure increases during mechanical breath delivery, venous return to the heart (preload) can be impeded, potentially leading to a decrease in cardiac output and systemic blood pressure, especially in volume-depleted patients. Understanding this mechanics helps nurses monitor vital signs meticulously and recognize how changes in ventilator parameters can instantly influence a patient's hemodynamic stability. Furthermore, awareness of lung compliance (the stretchability of the lungs) and airway resistance guides the nurse in identifying acute changes such as bronchospasm, mucus plugging, or tension pneumothorax during care.

headings.title: Modes of Mechanical Ventilation
headings.content: Modes of mechanical ventilation dictate how the ventilator interacts with the patient's spontaneous breathing efforts and determine the degree of machine assistance versus patient control. Understanding these modes is essential for clinical nurses monitoring intensive care unit patients. Controlled ventilation modes, such as Controlled Mandatory Ventilation (CMV), deliver a preset respiratory rate and tidal volume regardless of any breathing effort initiated by the patient; this mode is primarily used for completely paralyzed or heavily sedated patients. Assist-Control (AC) ventilation allows the patient to trigger breaths, but every triggered breath is delivered by the ventilator at a preset volume or pressure, ensuring full ventilatory support for each cycle. Synchronized Intermittent Mandatory Ventilation (SIMV) provides a set number of mandatory breaths synchronized with the patient's respiratory efforts, but allows the patient to breathe spontaneously between these mandatory breaths without machine assistance, making it useful for weaning protocols. Pressure Support Ventilation (PSV) is a spontaneous mode where the ventilator delivers a preset amount of positive pressure during inspiration only when triggered by the patient, helping to overcome the resistance of the endotracheal tube. Modern ventilators also feature advanced modes like Pressure Control Ventilation (PCV), which limits peak airway pressures to protect fragile lung tissues from barotrauma. Nursing students must be familiar with these modes to interpret ventilator alarms correctly, recognize patient-ventilator dyssynchrony, and report inappropriate respiratory work rates to the attending physician promptly.

headings.title: Ventilator Settings and Initial Setup
headings.content: Initiating mechanical ventilation requires careful calculation and programming of specific ventilator settings tailored to the individual patient's anthropometric measurements, underlying pathology, and blood gas results. Initial setup parameters typically include FiO2 (fraction of inspired oxygen), tidal volume (Vt), respiratory rate (RR), PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure), and inspiratory flow rate. The tidal volume is generally calculated based on the patient's predicted body weight (PBW) rather than actual weight, typically targeting 6 to 8 mL/kg to prevent volutrauma and overdistension of alveoli, especially in acute lung injury or ARDS. PEEP is applied at the end of expiration to keep alveoli open, prevent alveolar collapse, improve functional residual capacity, and enhance oxygenation; initial PEEP is usually set between 5 to 8 cmH2O. The FiO2 is adjusted to achieve adequate arterial oxygen saturation, starting high during emergency intubation and subsequently titrated down as quickly as safety permits to avoid oxygen toxicity. The respiratory rate is set to maintain normal minute ventilation and target a normal arterial carbon dioxide level (PaCO2), usually between 12 to 20 breaths per minute. Nurses play a vital role during initial setup by verifying physician orders, checking ventilator circuit integrity, ensuring manual resuscitation bags are connected to an oxygen source at the bedside, and assisting with baseline arterial blood gas (ABG) sampling 15 to 30 minutes after initiation to evaluate the efficacy of the selected settings.

headings.title: Patient Assessment and Monitoring
headings.content: Continuous patient assessment and rigorous monitoring are cornerstones of safe critical care nursing for individuals undergoing mechanical ventilation. Because the ventilator takes over a vital physiological function, nurses must regularly evaluate both the patient's clinical response and the mechanical performance of the equipment. Clinical assessment involves observing chest symmetry, monitoring respiratory rate and pattern, auscultating bilateral breath sounds to confirm proper endotracheal tube placement (ruling out mainstem bronchial intubation), and checking for signs of respiratory distress or cyanosis. Hemodynamic monitoring—including regular checks of heart rate, blood pressure, peripheral perfusion, and oxygen saturation via pulse oximetry—is essential to detect adverse cardiovascular effects resulting from positive pressure. Ventilator monitoring requires tracking peak inspiratory pressure (PIP) and plateau pressure to assess airway resistance and lung compliance changes. Alarms must never be silenced or ignored; nurses must investigate high-pressure alarms (which can indicate obstruction, coughing, secretions, or decreased compliance) and low-pressure alarms (which often signify disconnections, leaks, or extubation). Laboratory monitoring, particularly analyzing arterial blood gases (ABGs), provides objective data on oxygenation, ventilation, and acid-base status, guiding necessary adjustments in ventilator settings by the multidisciplinary team. Documentation of these assessments must be meticulous and performed at designated intervals per hospital policy.

headings.title: Nursing Care of the Mechanically Ventilated Patient
headings.content: Comprehensive nursing care for the mechanically ventilated patient extends far beyond operating the ventilator machinery, focusing on comfort, infection prevention, and complication mitigation. One of the highest priorities is preventing Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia (VAP), a serious hospital-acquired infection. Nurses implement the VAP bundle, which includes elevating the head of the bed between 30 and 45 degrees, performing daily sedative interruption trials and assessments of readiness to extubate, providing meticulous oral hygiene with chlorhexidine solutions, and maintaining proper endotracheal tube cuff pressures (typically between 20 to 30 cmH2O). Regular airway clearance via sterile suctioning is performed based on clinical indication—such as visible secretions, coughing, or coarse breath sounds—rather than routine schedules, taking care to pre-oxygenate the patient and limit suction duration to minimize hypoxia and mucosal trauma. Adequate humidification and warming of inspired gases are crucial to prevent drying of secretions and mucous plugging. Furthermore, nurses must provide frequent eye care to prevent corneal abrasions, reposition the patient every two hours to prevent pressure ulcers, and ensure passive or active range of motion exercises. Communication can be exceptionally frustrating for conscious ventilated patients; nurses should utilize alternative communication tools such as communication boards, writing pads, or hand gestures to alleviate anxiety and promote psychological well-being.

headings.title: Complications and Troubleshooting in Mechanical Ventilation
headings.content: Mechanical ventilation, while life-saving, carries significant risks of complications that require vigilant nursing surveillance and rapid troubleshooting skills. Barotrauma and volutrauma are major pulmonary complications caused by excessive positive pressure or over-distension of lung alveoli, which can lead to alveolar rupture, pneumothorax, subcutaneous emphysema, or pneumomediastinum. Nurses must immediately recognize signs of tension pneumothorax—such as sudden respiratory distress, asymmetrical chest expansion, absent breath sounds on the affected side, tracheal deviation, and rapid hemodynamic collapse—and prepare for emergency needle decompression or chest tube insertion. Oxygen toxicity can develop from prolonged exposure to high FiO2 levels (> 60%), resulting in pulmonary tissue damage and absorptive atelectasis. Cardiovascular complications, including hypotension and decreased cardiac output, occur due to elevated intrathoracic pressure impairing venous return. Gastrointestinal complications such as stress ulcers and ileus are common; thus, prophylactic medications like proton pump inhibitors and early enteral nutrition are frequently ordered. When troubleshooting ventilator alarms or sudden patient deterioration using the 'DOPE' mnemonic (Displacement of the tube, Obstruction of the tube, Pneumothorax, Equipment failure), the nurse must first disconnect the patient from the ventilator and manually ventilate them with a bag-valve-mask device using 100% oxygen if mechanical failure or severe distress is suspected, ensuring patient safety before diagnosing the equipment problem.

headings.title: Weaning Protocols and Extubation
headings.content: Weaning is the gradual process of transitioning a patient from mechanical ventilatory support back to spontaneous breathing, culminating in the removal of the artificial airway (extubation). The weaning process begins as soon as the underlying condition that necessitated mechanical ventilation has resolved or significantly improved. Nurses play an integral collaborative role by assessing readiness for weaning daily using standardized criteria, which include adequate oxygenation (e.g., PaO2/FiO2 ratio > 200 on low FiO2), stable cardiovascular status without high-dose vasopressors, adequate mental alertness, absence of excessive respiratory secretions, and successful completion of a Spontaneous Breathing Trial (SBT). During an SBT, the patient breathes with minimal or no ventilatory support (such as T-piece trial or low levels of pressure support with CPAP) for 30 to 120 minutes while being closely monitored for signs of weaning failure, which include tachypnea, tachycardia, hypertension, oxygen desaturation, diaphoresis, and severe anxiety. If the patient tolerates the SBT, the multidisciplinary team proceeds with extubation. Nursing responsibilities during extubation include explaining the procedure, suctioning the endotracheal tube and oropharynx thoroughly, defusing the cuff, removing the tube at peak inspiration or expiration as clinically guided, applying prescribed oxygen therapy via face mask or nasal cannula, and monitoring closely for post-extubation complications such as stridor (indicating upper airway edema), hoarseness, and aspiration.
